checks.title: Week 5: from phases to reactions
checks.source: Welcome to Week five, from phases to chemical reactions. This is our independent lesson for Friday, November sixth. We will meet onsite again on Friday, November thirteenth. Please begin with the short review in section R of the worksheet. Your recent questions showed that we should separate two ideas before moving on. Bulk phase equilibrium concerns a substance distributed between macroscopic phases, such as a solid and its vapor. Adsorption concerns uptake associated with a surface. The amount adsorbed depends on an adsorption relation and the available surface capacity. A vapor pressure alone does not describe that uptake. Today, we will use the same habit of combining an equilibrium relation with conservation, but the species can also react. Our main example is a synthetic dissociation, A two forming two A atoms. We will follow one worksheet and use Lab twelve. Keep the worksheet beside the video so every pause has a clear place to work.

checks.title: Partial and total pressure at fixed volume
checks.source: Before we discuss reactions, revisit pressure in a closed, rigid vessel. The temperature and the volume are fixed. The ideal gas equation connects the amount of each gas to its own partial pressure. Total pressure is the sum of those partial pressures. If all of the volatile solid has disappeared, calculate the volatile gas pressure from its available amount. Do not continue forcing its pressure to equal the saturation value after that phase is depleted. The assumption of an ideal gas is a separate modeling choice. Losing the solid phase does not make a real gas ideal. Now pause for four minutes and complete R one. Use the values printed in the worksheet, calculate the volatile partial pressure and total pressure, then state which pressure changes when inert gas is added at fixed temperature and volume. Keep the volatile inventory unchanged. Record a unit check. After your attempt, continue to the next question. We will check both review answers together.

checks.title: A balance needs an independent equation
checks.source: The next question concerns adsorption in a finite vessel. Conservation tells us that the feed is divided between free gas and adsorbed material. The Langmuir equation supplies another condition that the proposed state must satisfy. Choosing two amounts that add to the feed is insufficient if the adsorbed amount disagrees with the isotherm at the same pressure. In R two, the pressure and the model parameters are supplied. First calculate the gas amount from pressure, volume and temperature. Independently calculate the loading from the Langmuir equation, then multiply that loading by the adsorbent mass. Only after these two calculations should you compare their sum with the feed. Use units of mole per kilogram for the loading and kilograms for the adsorbent mass. Their product is an amount in moles. Pause for four minutes and complete R two. If a number seems unreasonable, write which equation or conversion you need to check. Continue when the time budget ends.

checks.title: Reaction extent keeps the atoms balanced
checks.source: Our reaction is A two gas in equilibrium with two A gas. We begin with one mole of A two and no A. No inert gas is present in the three required cases. A two contains two A atoms, so the reaction conserves atoms even though the number of gas molecules changes. Reaction extent tells us how far the reaction has proceeded on the written stoichiometric basis. Consuming one mole of A two produces two moles of A. The general expression is the initial amount plus the stoichiometric coefficient times the reaction extent. Reactant coefficients are negative and product coefficients are positive. For this particular feed, it is convenient to define f as the reaction extent divided by one mole. The fraction f is dimensionless. The amounts are one minus f moles of A two and two f moles of A. Nonnegative amounts require f between zero and one. These bounds come from the available material, before we use any equilibrium constant.

checks.title: Activities make Q dimensionless
checks.source: To describe equilibrium, we need activities. For today's ideal gas model, the activity of a species is its mole fraction multiplied by total pressure, divided by the standard pressure. Both pressures must use the same units. Their ratio is dimensionless, and so is the activity. We use a standard pressure of one hundred kilopascals throughout this lesson. This is a reference convention. The actual total pressure is a separate input that we can change. For A two dissociating into two A, the quotient is the activity of A squared, divided by the activity of A two. The exponents come directly from the reaction coefficients. Write this activity expression before substituting mole fractions. That step makes it easier to see how pressure enters the calculation. Later we will compare one hundred and four hundred kilopascals at the same temperature. Our standard pressure stays at one hundred kilopascals in both cases.

checks.title: Which way does the reaction proceed?
checks.source: How can the quotient tell us which direction is favored? At fixed temperature and pressure, the reaction Gibbs energy is the standard reaction Gibbs energy plus R T times the natural logarithm of Q. An equivalent form is R T times the natural logarithm of Q divided by K. A negative value favors forward reaction. A positive value favors reverse reaction. At an interior equilibrium, the reaction Gibbs energy is zero and Q equals K. These statements refer to the reaction as written. Reversing the reaction reverses the corresponding sign convention. For B one, use the supplied standard reaction Gibbs energy of minus four thousand joules per mole at three hundred and fifty kelvin. Test Q equal to one and Q equal to ten. Pause for six minutes, calculate the signs and write the favored direction for each state. Use the natural logarithm. We will return to these answers after calculating K by two routes.

checks.title: Route 1: K from standard Gibbs energy
checks.source: The first route starts with standard reaction Gibbs energy at the temperature of interest. The equation is natural log K equals minus standard reaction Gibbs energy divided by R T. For this example, the supplied standard reaction Gibbs energy applies at three hundred and fifty kelvin. It is minus four kilojoules per mole of reaction as written. To use the gas constant in joules per mole per kelvin, convert that energy to minus four thousand joules per mole. Keep the two minus signs separate until you substitute. A negative standard reaction Gibbs energy gives a positive natural logarithm of K, so K should exceed one. This sign prediction is a quick check on the arithmetic. The final equilibrium constant is dimensionless because it is defined using dimensionless activities. A larger K describes a stronger product preference in this convention, but it does not by itself specify the conversion. The feed and constraints are also needed.

checks.title: Both routes give the same reference K
checks.source: Both routes give a standard reaction Gibbs energy of minus four thousand joules per mole at three hundred and fifty kelvin. Dividing its negative by R T gives natural log K equal to about one point three seven four five four. Exponentiating gives K equal to about three point nine five three two six. It is the actual reaction Gibbs energy that becomes zero.

checks.title: Temperature changes the equilibrium constant
checks.source: We have changed pressure while holding K fixed. Next we change temperature. The standard equilibrium constant depends on temperature for a fixed reaction and standard-state convention. A Gibbs-energy value supplied at one temperature gives one point on that relationship. It does not automatically give a law for other temperatures. To estimate K at four hundred kelvin, we will use the reference constant at three hundred and fifty kelvin together with the standard reaction enthalpy. Our model assumes that the reaction enthalpy remains constant over this interval. This is an approximation with a stated range, rather than a new measured data set. Because the reaction enthalpy is positive, the dissociation is endothermic. Before using the equation, predict whether a higher temperature should increase or decrease the equilibrium constant. Keep pressure at one hundred kilopascals for the temperature case so the comparison isolates temperature. The initial feed and standard pressure also remain unchanged.

checks.title: Route 3: K at a new temperature
checks.source: The integrated van't Hoff equation relates the natural logarithm of the ratio of the two equilibrium constants to the reaction enthalpy. With constant enthalpy, it is the enthalpy divided by R, multiplied by one over the reference temperature minus one over the new temperature. Here the reference temperature is three hundred and fifty kelvin, and the new temperature is four hundred kelvin. Use fifty thousand joules per mole for the reaction enthalpy. Since the new temperature is higher, one over the reference temperature is larger than one over the new temperature. The difference is positive. The enthalpy is also positive, so the logarithm of the K ratio should be positive. That predicts an increase in K. To find the new natural logarithm of K, add this change to the reference natural logarithm. Then exponentiate once. Keep both temperatures in kelvin and check the sign before calculating the final value.

checks.source: Before the final form, check the explanation you would give to another student. K follows from standard thermodynamic properties and the chosen temperature. In a rigid ideal gas vessel at fixed temperature and volume, adding inert leaves reacting-species partial pressures unchanged, so an initially equilibrated reacting mixture does not shift.
